name: Wireless Security
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Compare WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3, Personal and Enterprise modes, and configure and verify a WPA2-PSK WLAN in the WLC GUI.

lesson.intro: A wired network at least makes an attacker find a jack. A wireless network broadcasts into the parking lot. This lesson explains how Wi-Fi security got from the broken WEP to WPA3, what SAE, forward secrecy and protected management frames add, the difference between Personal (pre-shared key) and Enterprise (802.1X with RADIUS) modes and the EAP methods behind Enterprise, what the 4-way handshake does, and then walks through building, verifying and troubleshooting a WPA2-PSK WLAN in a Cisco wireless LAN controller GUI, which the CCNA tests directly.
objectives: Explain why WEP failed and what WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 each changed
Describe WPA3's SAE, forward secrecy, protected management frames, 192-bit mode and transition mode
Compare Personal and Enterprise modes, name the 802.1X roles and compare the common EAP methods
Describe the 4-way handshake and why WPA2-Personal is exposed to offline dictionary attacks
Configure, verify and troubleshoot a WPA2-PSK WLAN in the WLC GUI, on AireOS and on a Catalyst 9800

sections.title: Why wireless needs its own security
sections.body:
A client in a coffee shop types a password into an unencrypted connection. The radio signal does not go only to the access point; it spreads out in every direction, and anyone within range with a laptop can capture the frames. There is no cable to trace and no port to lock.

Wireless security therefore has three jobs:

- **Authentication**: only trusted clients may join. Ideally the client also authenticates the network, because an attacker can run a fake AP with the same SSID (an evil twin) and become a man in the middle.
- **Privacy**: every data frame is encrypted before it goes on the air. The AP negotiates a unique key with each client for unicast traffic and uses a shared **group key** for broadcast and multicast frames.
- **Integrity**: a **message integrity check (MIC)** is computed over each frame, so the receiver can detect any tampering in transit.

The original 802.11 standard offered just two methods. **Open authentication** asks for no credentials at all; any 802.11 device may associate. It is used for guest networks, often with a web portal where users accept terms, but the data itself is not encrypted by open authentication. The other was WEP, the subject of the next section.

Two popular tricks are not real security. Hiding the SSID (not broadcasting it in beacons) does not stop anyone, because clients still send the name in their probes. And MAC address filtering is defeated by copying an allowed MAC. Real protection comes from strong authentication and encryption.

Wireless also has attacks with no wired equivalent. A **rogue AP** is an access point plugged into the network without permission, often by a well-meaning employee, which opens a back door around every wired control. An **evil twin** is an attacker's AP that copies a real SSID so clients connect to it and hand over their traffic. And because 802.11 management frames were originally unprotected, an attacker can forge **deauthentication** frames to kick clients off, either as a denial of service or to make them reconnect while the attacker records the handshake. Cisco WLCs detect rogue APs, Enterprise authentication with server certificate checks defeats evil twins, and protected management frames stop forged deauthentication.
sections.code:
Need             What it protects against                 Mechanism
Authentication   Unknown clients joining, fake APs        PSK/SAE or 802.1X/EAP
Privacy          Eavesdroppers in radio range             Encryption with per-client keys (AES)
Integrity        Frames altered in transit                Message integrity check (MIC)
sections.pitfall: Treating a hidden SSID or a MAC filter list as security. Both are trivial to bypass with a free wireless sniffer.

check.question: What does a message integrity check (MIC) add to a wireless frame?
choices: It hides the SSID from beacons
It lets the receiver detect whether the frame was altered in transit
It assigns the client an IP address
It authenticates the client to the RADIUS server
check.explanation: The MIC is computed over the frame's contents; if anything changes, the receiver's calculation no longer matches and the frame is rejected. Encryption provides privacy, not tamper detection.

sections.title: WEP and why it failed
sections.body:
**Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP)** was part of the original 802.11 standard in 1999. It encrypted frames with the **RC4** stream cipher using a static key of 40 or 104 bits (typed as 10 or 26 hex digits) that was configured on the AP and on every client. Vendors called these 64-bit and 128-bit WEP because a 24-bit **initialization vector (IV)** was added to the key for each frame. The same key could also be used for shared-key authentication, where the AP sent a challenge and the client returned it encrypted.

WEP failed on several fronts at once:

- The **24-bit IV** is tiny and sent in clear text. On a busy WLAN, IVs repeat within hours, and combined with weaknesses in how WEP fed keys to RC4, an attacker who collects enough frames can recover the key, in minutes with modern tools.
- The key is **static and shared**. Every user has the same key, it never changes on its own, and replacing it means touching every device.
- Its integrity check is a simple CRC-32 checksum, not a cryptographic MIC, so attackers can modify frames without being detected.
- Shared-key authentication actually helps the attacker, because capturing the challenge and its encrypted response leaks keystream.

The weaknesses were published in 2001, and the 802.11i amendment (2004) officially deprecated WEP. Making the key longer (128-bit WEP) does not fix any of these problems. If a device can only do WEP, it should not be on your network.
sections.code:
WEP at a glance
  Cipher       RC4 stream cipher
  Key          static 40-bit or 104-bit key typed on every device
               (10 or 26 hex digits; "64/128-bit" includes the IV)
  IV           24 bits, sent in clear, repeats quickly on a busy WLAN
  Integrity    CRC-32 checksum, not a cryptographic MIC
  Status       broken in 2001, deprecated by 802.11i in 2004
sections.pitfall: Assuming 128-bit WEP is acceptable because the number looks big. The flaws are in the design (short IV, static shared key, weak integrity), so key length does not help.

check.question: Which WEP weakness lets attackers recover the key by collecting enough traffic?
choices: It uses AES with too short a key
Its short 24-bit IV, sent in clear, repeats with a static shared key
check.explanation: With only 24 bits, IVs repeat quickly, and with one static key for everyone, the repeated IVs and RC4 key weaknesses let tools derive the key. WEP uses RC4, not AES, and needs no RADIUS server.

sections.title: WPA and WPA2
sections.body:
Rather than ask you to pick ciphers and methods one by one, the **Wi-Fi Alliance** certifies devices for three generations of **Wi-Fi Protected Access**. If the client and the AP or WLC are certified for the same version, they interoperate securely, and every version supports a **Personal** mode (a shared key) and an **Enterprise** mode (802.1X).

**WPA** (2003) was a stopgap built from a draft of the IEEE 802.11i amendment so that existing WEP hardware could be upgraded with firmware. Its main tool is **TKIP** (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol), which still uses RC4 because that is what WEP chips could do, but wraps it in fixes: a fresh key for every frame, an IV doubled to 48 bits, a sequence counter against replays and a real message integrity check (nicknamed Michael). TKIP was later attacked too and was deprecated in the 802.11-2012 standard.

**WPA2** (2004) implements the full 802.11i standard and is built around **CCMP**: AES in counter mode for encryption plus CBC-MAC for the integrity check, so the pair is usually written **AES-CCMP**. AES runs in hardware, so WPA2 needed new chips, and it has been the baseline for well over a decade. WPA could optionally use CCMP as well, but TKIP is what defines it on the exam.

The line to remember: WEP used RC4 with a static key; WPA used TKIP, still RC4 underneath; WPA2 uses AES-CCMP; WPA3 adds a stronger key exchange and GCMP (next section). When you configure a WLAN, choose WPA2 with AES only. Enabling TKIP for one old device weakens the WLAN for everyone, and TKIP clients are held to slow legacy data rates.
sections.code:
WPA (2003)         WPA2 (2004)        WPA3 (2018)
Based on                  Draft 802.11i      Full 802.11i       WPA2 plus new protections
Encryption and MIC        TKIP (RC4-based)   AES-CCMP           AES-GCMP (as the CCNA pairs it)
Personal authentication   PSK                PSK                SAE
Enterprise authentication 802.1X/EAP         802.1X/EAP         802.1X/EAP
Protected mgmt frames     No                 Optional           Required
Status                    Deprecated         Widely deployed    Current best choice
sections.tip: A quick mapping for the exam: WEP = RC4 static key, WPA = TKIP, WPA2 = AES-CCMP, WPA3 = SAE plus PMF (and GCMP).
sections.pitfall: Selecting WPA2 with TKIP for compatibility. TKIP is deprecated and also limits 802.11n and newer clients to slow legacy data rates; use AES only.

check.question: Which encryption and integrity method is required by WPA2?
check.explanation: WPA2 implements the full 802.11i standard with AES-CCMP. TKIP belongs to WPA, and RC4 with a static key is WEP.

sections.title: WPA3: SAE, forward secrecy and protected management frames
sections.body:
**WPA3** (2018) keeps AES and fixes the weaknesses that remained in WPA2. Four features matter for the exam.

- **SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)** replaces the PSK exchange in WPA3-Personal. Both sides prove they know the password through an exchange, based on the Dragonfly handshake, that gives an eavesdropper nothing to test guesses against. Every guess needs a fresh live exchange with the AP, so the offline dictionary attack against captured WPA2 handshakes stops working. The 4-way handshake still runs afterward to derive the session keys.
- **Forward secrecy**: each SAE exchange produces a fresh, unique PMK, so if the passphrase leaks later, traffic recorded earlier still cannot be decrypted with it.
- **Protected Management Frames (PMF, from 802.11w)** are mandatory. Management frames such as deauthentication and disassociation are protected, so an attacker can no longer kick clients off by forging them. In WPA2, PMF is optional.
- **Stronger encryption**: Cisco's CCNA material pairs WPA3 with **AES-GCMP**. In practice, WPA3-Personal and ordinary WPA3-Enterprise still use AES-CCMP-128, while the optional **WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode** requires GCMP-256 with 384-bit elliptic curve cryptography and SHA-384, aimed at government and finance networks. On the exam, pair WPA3 with GCMP.

Most networks move to WPA3 gradually. **WPA2/WPA3 transition mode** runs one SSID where WPA3 clients use SAE and WPA2 clients use the PSK with the same passphrase, with PMF optional so older clients can still join. For open guest networks, the Wi-Fi Alliance's **Enhanced Open** (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, OWE) encrypts each client's traffic without any password, though it does not prove which network you joined.
sections.code:
WPA2-Personal                  WPA3-Personal
Key exchange          PSK, then 4-way handshake      SAE, then 4-way handshake
Offline guessing      Possible from one capture      Not possible; every guess is live
Forward secrecy       No                             Yes
PMF                   Optional                       Required

WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode: GCMP-256, SHA-384, 384-bit ECDH and ECDSA
Transition mode: one SSID; WPA3 clients use SAE, WPA2 clients use the PSK

activity.title: Secure a WLAN with WPA3
activity.prompt: Use the controller GUI to protect the WLAN with WPA3: choose WPA3 with SAE key management, make sure protected management frames are required, set a strong passphrase and test the client join. Then ask yourself what an older WPA2-only client would need, and which settings transition mode relaxes.

sections.pitfall: Expecting WPA3 to make a weak passphrase safe. SAE stops offline guessing, but anyone who knows or guesses the passphrase online can still join; use long passphrases, or Enterprise mode for staff.

check.question: What does forward secrecy in WPA3-Personal guarantee?
choices: The passphrase can never be guessed, even online
Traffic recorded before a passphrase leak cannot be decrypted with that passphrase later
The AP changes the SSID every day
check.explanation: Each SAE exchange creates its own PMK, so knowing the passphrase does not reveal the keys of earlier sessions. With WPA2-Personal, an attacker who learns the passphrase can decrypt any recorded session whose handshake was captured.

sections.title: Personal versus Enterprise
sections.body:
**Personal mode** uses one **pre-shared key (PSK)**: a passphrase of 8 to 63 ASCII characters (or 64 hex digits) configured on the AP or WLC and on every client. It is simple and needs no servers, which makes it right for homes, small offices and devices such as printers and sensors that cannot do anything fancier. The costs show up as the network grows: everybody shares one secret, an employee who leaves still knows it, changing it means reconfiguring every device, nobody is individually accountable, and with WPA2 the shared key can be attacked offline (see the 4-way handshake section).

**Enterprise mode** authenticates every user or device individually with **802.1X** and the **Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)**, against a central **RADIUS** server such as Cisco ISE. 802.1X defines three roles:

- **Supplicant**: the client device asking for access.
- **Authenticator**: the network device controlling access; in a controller-based design, the **WLC** with its APs.
- **Authentication server (AS)**: usually a RADIUS server that checks the credentials against a user database and policies.

Enterprise gives per-user credentials you can revoke individually, a unique key for every session, and accounting of who connected when. That is why it is the normal choice for corporate WLANs, and why a new WLAN on a Cisco WLC defaults to WPA2 with 802.1X. Choose Personal only where a RADIUS server is not practical: small sites, guest-style networks or headless devices.
sections.code:
Supplicant           Authenticator                Authentication server
(laptop)  ~~~~~~~~~  AP ===CAPWAP=== WLC ------------ RADIUS server (Cisco ISE)
          802.11 open association,      RADIUS (UDP 1812)
          then EAP over the air         carries the EAP exchange

Until 802.1X succeeds, only EAP traffic from the supplicant is allowed.
sections.pitfall: Thinking the AP or WLC checks the user's password in Enterprise mode. The authenticator only relays EAP; the RADIUS server makes the decision.

check.question: In a WPA2-Enterprise WLAN using a Cisco WLC, which device plays the 802.1X authenticator role?
check.explanation: The WLC (with its APs) controls access and relays EAP between the client and the server, which makes it the authenticator. The laptop is the supplicant and the RADIUS server is the authentication server.

sections.title: 802.1X and EAP methods
sections.body:
In Enterprise mode the client first associates using open authentication, but until 802.1X succeeds the authenticator passes only EAP messages, relaying them to the RADIUS server inside RADIUS packets. The sequence:

1. The client associates with the AP, and the WLC sends an EAP identity request that the client answers.
2. The WLC relays the EAP exchange between the client and the RADIUS server. The chosen EAP method runs end to end between those two.
3. If the credentials are good, the server sends a RADIUS Access-Accept that includes keying material for the **pairwise master key (PMK)**, unique to this user and session.
4. The client and the authenticator run the 4-way handshake to derive the session keys, and encrypted data starts to flow.

EAP is a framework, so the method decides how the client proves itself:

- **EAP-TLS**: certificates on both the server and every client. The strongest choice, but you need a PKI to issue and revoke client certificates.
- **PEAP**: only the server has a certificate. The client verifies it, a TLS tunnel is built, and the client proves itself inside the tunnel, typically with a username and password (MSCHAPv2).
- **EAP-TTLS**: like PEAP, an outer TLS tunnel built with the server's certificate, with a wider choice of inner methods.
- **EAP-FAST**: Cisco's method, which builds the tunnel with a **protected access credential (PAC)** instead of requiring certificates.
- **LEAP**: an early Cisco method based on a weak password exchange, now deprecated.

Whatever the method, clients should validate the server's certificate. A client that skips that check will happily send its credentials to an evil twin running its own RADIUS server.
sections.code:
Method     Server cert   Client proves itself with        Notes
EAP-TLS    Yes           Its own certificate              Strongest; needs a client PKI
PEAP       Yes           Password inside a TLS tunnel     Very common (MSCHAPv2 inside)
EAP-TTLS   Yes           Various inner methods            Like PEAP, more flexible
EAP-FAST   Not required  Password inside a PAC tunnel     Cisco
LEAP       No            Weak password exchange           Deprecated
sections.pitfall: Skipping server certificate validation on clients. Without it, PEAP users will send their credentials to any evil twin that presents its own RADIUS server.

check.question: With PEAP, which side must have a certificate?
choices: Both the client and the server
check.explanation: PEAP builds its TLS tunnel with the server's certificate, and the client authenticates inside the tunnel with a password. EAP-TLS needs certificates on both sides, and EAP-FAST uses a PAC.

sections.title: The 4-way handshake
sections.body:
Both modes end the same way. Once the client is authenticated, the client and the AP share a **pairwise master key (PMK)**. In Personal mode the PMK is derived from the passphrase and the SSID, so every client ends up with the same PMK. In Enterprise mode it comes out of the 802.1X/EAP exchange, unique to each user and session.

The PMK is never used directly. The **4-way handshake** turns it into fresh session keys:

1. The AP sends a random number, the **ANonce**.
2. The client picks its own random **SNonce** and computes the **pairwise transient key (PTK)** from the PMK, both nonces and both MAC addresses. It sends the SNonce plus a MIC computed with the new key.
3. The AP computes the same PTK and checks the MIC; a valid MIC proves the client knows the PMK. The AP sends the **group temporal key (GTK)**, encrypted, plus its own MIC.
4. The client confirms, and both install the keys.

The PTK encrypts unicast frames between this client and the AP; the GTK encrypts broadcast and multicast frames for all clients. Notice what never crosses the air: the passphrase and the PMK.

There is still a weakness in **WPA2-Personal**. An attacker who records one handshake has the nonces, the MAC addresses and a MIC. Offline, the attacker can guess passphrases, compute the PTK for each guess and check it against the captured MIC, as fast as their hardware allows, with no lockout. Short or common passphrases fall quickly. Defenses: long random passphrases, or **WPA3-SAE**, where each guess requires a live exchange with the AP, so offline guessing does not work.
sections.code:
Client (supplicant)                                    AP / WLC (authenticator)
 Both already hold the PMK (from the passphrase, or from 802.1X/EAP)
  1.  <-------------------- ANonce -------------------------
      client derives PTK from PMK + ANonce + SNonce + both MACs
  2.  --------------------- SNonce + MIC ------------------>
      AP derives the same PTK and checks the MIC
  3.  <-------------------- GTK (encrypted) + MIC ----------
  4.  --------------------- ACK + MIC --------------------->
 Unicast now encrypted with the PTK; broadcast and multicast with the GTK
sections.pitfall: Believing the passphrase is sent to the AP during association. It never is; the MIC in message 2 proves the client knows it without revealing it.

check.question: In the 4-way handshake, how does the AP know the client has the correct pre-shared key?
choices: The client sends the passphrase encrypted in message 2
The client's MIC in message 2 verifies with the PTK the AP computed from the same PMK
The AP compares the client's MAC with an allowed list
check.explanation: Both sides derive the PTK from the PMK and the exchanged nonces. A MIC that verifies proves the client derived the same key, so it must know the PSK, and the key itself never crosses the air.

sections.title: Configuring a WPA2-PSK WLAN in the WLC GUI
sections.body:
The CCNA expects you to know the steps and settings for building a WLAN with WPA2 Personal in a controller's web GUI. Before you start, decide three things: the **SSID**, the **VLAN** (and so the controller interface) where its clients will live, and the **security** settings. The steps below follow the classic Cisco WLC (AireOS) GUI used in the official guide; a Catalyst 9800 controller offers the same choices under Configuration > Tags & Profiles > WLANs.

1. **Create a dynamic interface** for the client VLAN: Controller > Interfaces > New. Enter an interface name and the VLAN ID, apply, then set the interface's IP address, netmask, gateway and the primary (and optional secondary) DHCP server that the controller will relay client requests to. A dynamic interface is what maps a WLAN to a wired VLAN.
2. **Create the WLAN**: WLANs > Create New > Go. Choose type WLAN, enter a profile name and the SSID (often the same text), keep or pick the WLAN ID, and click Apply.
3. **General tab**: check Status Enabled, set the Radio Policy (all bands, or limit it to one), select the dynamic interface under Interface/Interface Group, and leave Broadcast SSID checked.
4. **Security tab, Layer 2**: set Layer 2 Security to WPA+WPA2. Under WPA+WPA2 Parameters, check WPA2 Policy (leave WPA unchecked) and WPA2 Encryption AES (leave TKIP unchecked). Under Authentication Key Management, uncheck 802.1X (the default for a new WLAN) and enable PSK. Set PSK Format to ASCII and type the passphrase (8 to 63 characters). No RADIUS server and no Layer 3 (web) security are needed for PSK.
5. **QoS tab**: Silver (best effort) is the default; Platinum is for voice, Gold for video, Bronze for background traffic.
6. **Advanced tab**: the defaults are fine for the exam, including a session timeout of 1800 seconds and client exclusion of misbehaving clients.
7. Click **Apply**, then **Save Configuration** so the WLAN survives a controller reboot.

For WPA2-Enterprise instead, you would first define the RADIUS server under Security > AAA > RADIUS > Authentication (IP address, shared secret, port 1812, status enabled), choose 802.1X rather than PSK under Authentication Key Management, and pick up to six servers on the WLAN's Security > AAA Servers tab.
sections.code:
Tab / page               Setting                          Value for WPA2-Personal
Controller > Interfaces  Dynamic interface                Name, VLAN ID, IP, mask, gateway, DHCP server
WLANs > Create New       Type / Profile Name / SSID / ID  WLAN / Staff / Staff / 1
General                  Status                           Enabled
General                  Interface/Interface Group(G)     The dynamic interface for the client VLAN
General                  Broadcast SSID                   Checked
Security > Layer 2       Layer 2 Security                 WPA+WPA2
Security > Layer 2       WPA2 Policy / Encryption         WPA2 checked, AES checked (no WPA, no TKIP)
Security > Layer 2       Auth Key Management              PSK enabled, 802.1X unchecked
Security > Layer 2       PSK Format and key               ASCII, 8 to 63 character passphrase
QoS                      Quality of Service               Silver (default), Platinum for voice

activity.title: Build the WPA2-PSK WLAN
activity.prompt: Create a WLAN for the Staff SSID, map it to the staff VLAN interface, secure it with WPA2, AES and a pre-shared key, then save and test a client join. Before you apply, predict what the WLANs page should show under Security Policies.

sections.pitfall: Leaving 802.1X checked under Authentication Key Management. A new WLAN defaults to WPA2 with 802.1X, so without changing it to PSK the WLAN expects a RADIUS server and passphrase clients cannot join.

check.question: You are building a WPA2-Personal WLAN on a WLC. Under Authentication Key Management on the Layer 2 security tab, what should be selected?
choices: Both 802.1X and PSK, with a RADIUS server
Neither; the passphrase goes on the Layer 3 tab
check.explanation: WPA2-Personal means pre-shared key authentication, so PSK is enabled and 802.1X (the default, used for WPA2-Enterprise) is unchecked. Layer 3 security is for web authentication, not the passphrase.

sections.title: The same WLAN on a Catalyst 9800 controller
sections.body:
Cisco's current controllers, the Catalyst 9800 series running IOS XE, ask the same questions in a different layout. Instead of one WLAN page that holds everything, the 9800 splits the settings into profiles and tags:

- The **WLAN profile** (Configuration > Tags & Profiles > WLANs) holds the SSID, the WLAN ID, the status and the security. On its Security > Layer2 tab you choose WPA2 (or WPA2 + WPA3, or WPA3), AES (CCMP128) encryption, PSK as the authentication key management, the pre-shared key itself, and the PMF setting.
- The **policy profile** (Configuration > Tags & Profiles > Policy) decides how client traffic is handled, most importantly the **VLAN** on its Access Policies tab. This replaces mapping the WLAN to a dynamic interface.
- The **policy tag** (Configuration > Tags & Profiles > Tags) pairs the WLAN profile with the policy profile.
- The policy tag is then **assigned to the APs** that should broadcast the SSID. The built-in default-policy-tag maps WLANs with IDs 1 to 16 to the default policy profile, which is why a quick lab WLAN can appear without any tagging.

The decisions are the same as in the AireOS steps: an SSID, a VLAN for the clients, WPA2 with AES and a PSK of 8 to 63 characters, then apply and save. Only the place each setting lives has moved. The 9800 also offers a Wireless Setup wizard that walks through the same objects in order. If a WLAN exists but no AP broadcasts it, follow the chain: is the WLAN enabled, is it in a policy tag, and is that tag on the APs?
sections.code:
AireOS WLC (CCNA guide)                  Catalyst 9800 (IOS XE)
WLANs > Create New                       Tags & Profiles > WLANs > Add (WLAN profile)
General: SSID, Status, Broadcast SSID    General: SSID, WLAN ID, Status, Broadcast SSID
Security > Layer 2: WPA2, AES, PSK       Security > Layer2: WPA2, AES(CCMP128), PSK, key
General: Interface (dynamic interface)   Policy profile > Access Policies: VLAN
WLAN is pushed to the joined APs         Policy tag (WLAN profile + policy profile),
                                         assigned to the APs
Apply, then Save Configuration           Apply to Device, then save the configuration
sections.pitfall: Creating the WLAN profile and stopping there. On a 9800 the SSID goes on the air only when a policy tag links it to a policy profile and that tag is on the APs, unless its WLAN ID falls under the default policy tag.

check.question: On a Catalyst 9800 controller, where do you set the VLAN that a WLAN's clients are placed in?
choices: In the WLAN profile's Security tab
check.explanation: The policy profile holds client traffic settings such as the VLAN. The WLAN profile holds the SSID and security, and the policy tag joins the two.

sections.title: Verifying and troubleshooting the WLAN
sections.body:
After you apply the configuration, check it from the controller's point of view before blaming the clients.

The **WLANs** page lists each WLAN with its ID, profile name, SSID, **Admin Status** (Enabled) and **Security Policies**. A correct WPA2-Personal WLAN shows `[WPA2][Auth(PSK)]`; if you see `Auth(802.1X)`, the key management setting was not changed. **Monitor > Clients** lists associated clients with their MAC address, the AP they joined, the WLAN profile and their status, and the client detail page shows the IP address the client received.

Most problems fall into a few patterns:

- **The SSID does not appear** on clients: the WLAN is not enabled, Broadcast SSID is unchecked, the radio policy excludes the client's band, or no AP has joined the controller.
- **The client sees the SSID but cannot join**: a wrong passphrase (the most common cause), a client that does not support WPA2 with AES, or the WLAN still set to 802.1X.
- **The client joins but gets no usable IP address** (for example a 169.254.x.x address): the WLAN is mapped to the wrong interface, the dynamic interface has the wrong VLAN or DHCP server, or the switch trunk to the WLC does not carry that VLAN. This is a wired problem, not a security one.
- **A client that mistyped the passphrase several times still cannot join for about a minute after fixing it**: client exclusion. By default the WLC excludes a client for 60 seconds after repeated authentication failures, a deliberate brake on password guessing.
- **You cannot reach the controller GUI from a wireless client**: by default the WLC refuses management sessions that come in through a WLAN. That is a deliberate security choice; it is changed globally under Management > Mgmt Via Wireless if really needed.
sections.code:
Symptom                              Check first
SSID not visible                     WLAN Status Enabled? Broadcast SSID? Radio policy? APs joined?
Sees SSID, cannot authenticate       Passphrase, WPA2 + AES on client, PSK (not 802.1X) selected
Associated but 169.254.x.x address   Interface/VLAN mapping, dynamic interface DHCP server, trunk VLANs
No GUI access from wireless client   Mgmt Via Wireless is disabled by default

Expected on the WLANs page:  Admin Status Enabled   Security Policies [WPA2][Auth(PSK)]

activity.title: Fix a broken WLAN
activity.prompt: This controller has a WLAN that clients cannot use. Sort the symptom first: can the client see the SSID, does it fail to authenticate, or does it join without a usable address? Then find the setting behind it in the GUI, fix it and test the client join again.

sections.pitfall: Changing the passphrase when clients associate but get no address. A client that successfully associated already passed the PSK check; look at the interface, VLAN and DHCP path instead.

check.question: Clients join a new WPA2-PSK WLAN successfully but all receive 169.254.x.x addresses. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The WLAN uses AES instead of TKIP
The WLAN's interface, VLAN or DHCP server mapping is wrong
check.explanation: Joining proves the PSK and security settings work. A self-assigned address means DHCP failed, which points to the WLAN-to-interface mapping, the VLAN or the DHCP server on the dynamic interface.

keyTerms.definition: Wired Equivalent Privacy: the original 802.11 encryption using RC4, a static shared key and a 24-bit IV; broken and deprecated.
Temporal Key Integrity Protocol: WPA's RC4-based stopgap with per-frame keys and a MIC; now deprecated.
The encryption (AES counter mode) and integrity (CBC-MAC) method required by WPA2.
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: WPA3-Personal's key exchange that resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy.
Protection for 802.11 management frames such as deauthentication; required in WPA3.
A passphrase of 8 to 63 characters shared by the AP or WLC and every client in Personal mode.
Port-based access control that authenticates each user or device through EAP before allowing traffic; used in Enterprise mode.
The client device requesting access in 802.1X.
The device that controls access and relays EAP in 802.1X, such as an AP or WLC.
The exchange that derives the session keys (PTK and GTK) from the PMK using two nonces, without sending the key itself.
A WLC interface that maps a WLAN to a wired VLAN, with its own IP address and DHCP server settings.
A property of WPA3 SAE: a later passphrase leak does not let an attacker decrypt traffic recorded earlier.
A WPA2/WPA3 mixed setting where WPA3 clients use SAE and WPA2 clients use the PSK on the same SSID.
EAP method with certificates on both the server and the client; the strongest common method.
EAP method where only the server has a certificate and the client authenticates with a password inside a TLS tunnel.
An attacker's AP that copies a legitimate SSID to lure clients into connecting through it.
Catalyst 9800 object that holds client traffic settings, such as the VLAN, for WLANs it is paired with in a policy tag.

summary: Wireless security needs authentication, privacy (encryption) and integrity (MIC); hidden SSIDs and MAC filters are not real protection, and rogue APs, evil twins and forged deauthentication are wireless-specific threats.
WEP (RC4, static key, 24-bit IV) is broken; WPA used TKIP as a stopgap; WPA2 uses AES-CCMP; WPA3 adds SAE, forward secrecy, required PMF and GCMP (GCMP-256 in 192-bit mode).
Personal mode shares one PSK; Enterprise mode uses 802.1X/EAP with a supplicant, an authenticator (the WLC) and a RADIUS server; EAP-TLS, PEAP and EAP-FAST differ in who needs a certificate.
The 4-way handshake derives the PTK and GTK from the PMK without sending the key; WPA2-Personal handshakes can be attacked offline, which SAE prevents.

AireOS: create a dynamic interface and the WLAN, enable it and map the interface, then set WPA2 + AES + PSK; a 9800 splits this into a WLAN profile, a policy profile (VLAN) and a policy tag on the APs.
Verify Security Policies [WPA2][Auth(PSK)] and Admin Status Enabled; no IP address means an interface, VLAN or DHCP problem, and repeated failures trigger 60 seconds of client exclusion.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a small business owner why their old WEP network is unsafe, what WPA2-Personal and WPA3 each do better (including SAE and protected management frames), when they should move to WPA2-Enterprise with a RADIUS server, and the settings you would choose when creating their new WPA2-PSK WLAN on a Cisco controller.

questions.question: Why must wireless data frames be encrypted even inside a company building?
choices: Radio signals reach anyone in range, who can capture the frames
Access points cannot forward unencrypted frames
Encryption is needed to assign IP addresses
questions.explanation: Radio spreads beyond walls and cannot be confined to authorized users, so any receiver in range can capture frames unless they are encrypted.

questions.question: Which two measures provide little real security on a WLAN? (Choose two.)
choices: Hiding the SSID by not broadcasting it
Allowing only a list of client MAC addresses
questions.explanation: Clients reveal hidden SSIDs in their probes, and allowed MAC addresses can be sniffed and copied. Strong authentication and AES encryption are what actually protect the WLAN.

questions.question: A guest WLAN uses open authentication with a web portal where users accept the terms of use. What protection does this give the guests' wireless data?
choices: AES encryption with a per-session key
None; open authentication does not encrypt data over the air
questions.explanation: Open authentication requires no credentials and provides no encryption. The web portal controls access to the network, not the privacy of the radio link.

questions.question: Which cipher does WEP use?
questions.explanation: WEP uses the RC4 stream cipher with a static key. AES arrived with WPA2 (CCMP) and GCMP with WPA3.

questions.question: How many bits long is the WEP initialization vector, the field whose small size lets IVs repeat quickly?
questions.explanation: WEP's IV is only 24 bits and is sent in clear text. TKIP later doubled it to 48 bits.

questions.question: Which three are design weaknesses of WEP? (Choose three.)
choices: A short 24-bit IV that repeats on busy networks
One static key shared by every user
A CRC-32 integrity check that is not cryptographic
It uses AES, which is too slow for wireless
questions.explanation: Short IVs, a static shared key and a non-cryptographic integrity check together make WEP crackable and forgeable. WEP needs no RADIUS server and uses RC4, not AES.

questions.question: Match each wireless security standard to the method most associated with it.

pairs.right: RC4 with a static shared key
SAE and required protected management frames

questions.explanation: Each generation replaced the weak point of the previous one: WEP's static RC4 key, then TKIP as a stopgap, then AES-CCMP, then SAE with PMF.

questions.question: Which encryption method does WPA2 require?
questions.explanation: WPA2 implements the full 802.11i standard, which requires AES-CCMP for encryption and integrity.

questions.question: Why was TKIP designed to keep using the RC4 cipher?
choices: So existing WEP hardware could be upgraded to WPA with a firmware update
Because RADIUS servers only support RC4
questions.explanation: WEP adapters had RC4 built into hardware. TKIP added per-frame keys, a longer IV and a MIC on top of RC4 so that hardware could be upgraded rather than replaced, buying time until AES-based WPA2.

questions.question: Which three improvements does WPA3 bring over WPA2? (Choose three.)
choices: SAE replaces the PSK exchange in Personal mode
TKIP is reintroduced for older clients
questions.explanation: WPA3 adds SAE (with forward secrecy) and makes PMF mandatory. It does not bring back TKIP, and Enterprise mode still uses 802.1X.

questions.question: An attacker repeatedly sends forged deauthentication frames to disconnect clients from an AP. Which WPA3 feature is designed to stop this?
questions.explanation: PMF authenticates management frames such as deauthentication, so forged ones are ignored. WPA3 makes PMF mandatory.

questions.question: A warehouse has one old barcode scanner that supports only WPA with TKIP. Every other device supports WPA2 with AES. What is the best approach?
choices: Enable WPA and TKIP alongside WPA2 on the main WLAN
Switch the main WLAN to WEP so everything connects
Keep the main WLAN on WPA2 with AES only, and replace or isolate the legacy scanner
Use open authentication with MAC filtering for all devices
questions.explanation: Adding TKIP weakens the WLAN for everyone and slows newer clients; WEP and open authentication are worse. Replace the scanner, or isolate it on its own restricted WLAN while it is phased out.

questions.question: Match each 802.1X role to the device that plays it in a controller-based WLAN.

pairs.right: The RADIUS server, such as Cisco ISE

questions.explanation: The supplicant requests access, the authenticator controls the port and relays EAP, and the authentication server checks credentials and decides.

questions.question: A company with 2,000 employees, regular staff turnover and an existing RADIUS server is designing its corporate WLAN. Which mode fits best?
choices: Open authentication with a hidden SSID
questions.explanation: Enterprise mode gives every user their own credentials that can be revoked individually when they leave. A shared PSK would have to be changed on every device each time someone left.

questions.question: Which EAP method requires a digital certificate on the authentication server and on every client device?
questions.explanation: EAP-TLS uses certificates on both sides for mutual authentication, which is why it needs a PKI. PEAP needs only a server certificate, and EAP-FAST uses a PAC.

questions.question: With PEAP, how does the client prove its identity?
choices: With a username and password sent inside a TLS tunnel built using the server's certificate
questions.explanation: In PEAP only the server has a certificate. The client verifies it, a TLS tunnel is built, and the client then authenticates inside the tunnel, typically with MSCHAPv2.

questions.question: A laptop has associated to a WPA2-Enterprise WLAN but 802.1X authentication has not finished yet. What traffic can it send through the authenticator?
choices: All traffic except to other wireless clients
Only EAP messages, which are relayed to the RADIUS server
Any traffic, because association already succeeded
questions.explanation: 802.1X blocks everything except EAP until authentication succeeds. The client cannot even get an IP address before it is authenticated.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of characters for an ASCII WPA2 pre-shared key passphrase?
questions.explanation: An ASCII passphrase must be 8 to 63 characters (or exactly 64 hex digits). Longer random passphrases resist offline guessing far better.

questions.question: Put the messages of the 4-way handshake in order.
items: AP sends its ANonce to the client
Client derives the PTK and sends its SNonce with a MIC
AP derives the same PTK, checks the MIC and sends the encrypted GTK with a MIC
Client acknowledges and both install the keys
questions.explanation: Each side needs both nonces to compute the PTK, so the AP's nonce goes first and the client's second. The GTK can only be sent once a PTK exists to encrypt it.

questions.question: Which key encrypts broadcast and multicast frames that the AP sends to all of its clients?
questions.explanation: The group temporal key is shared by all clients of the AP for broadcast and multicast. Each client's PTK protects only its own unicast traffic.

questions.question: An attacker sits outside an office running WPA2-Personal and records one client joining. What can the attacker now do with that capture?
choices: Read the passphrase directly from message 2
Nothing, because the handshake contains no useful information
Join the WLAN immediately using the captured MIC
Guess passphrases offline and check each guess against the captured MIC
questions.explanation: The capture contains the nonces, MAC addresses and a MIC. For each guessed passphrase the attacker can compute the PTK and test the MIC, with no lockout. WPA3-SAE prevents this offline guessing.

questions.question: Why does WPA3-SAE resist offline dictionary attacks on the passphrase?
choices: Each password guess requires a live exchange with the AP, so captured traffic cannot be used to test guesses
SAE sends the passphrase encrypted with AES
SAE forces passphrases to be at least 63 characters
questions.explanation: SAE's exchange does not give an eavesdropper anything to test guesses against offline. An attacker must interact with the AP for each guess, which is slow and detectable.

questions.question: In WPA2-Personal, where does the PMK come from, and is it ever sent over the air?
questions.answer: The PMK is derived from the pre-shared passphrase and the SSID, so all clients of that WLAN share it. It is never sent over the air; the 4-way handshake derives session keys from it and proves knowledge of it with MICs.
questions.explanation: Because every client shares the same PMK in Personal mode, a captured handshake is enough to attack the passphrase offline.

questions.question: Put these WLC GUI steps for a new WPA2-PSK WLAN in a working order.
items: Create a dynamic interface for the client VLAN under Controller > Interfaces
Create the WLAN under WLANs > Create New with a profile name and SSID
On the General tab, enable the WLAN and select the dynamic interface
On the Security > Layer 2 tab, choose WPA2 with AES and PSK, and enter the passphrase
Click Apply and save the configuration
questions.explanation: The interface must exist before the WLAN can be mapped to it. Security is set on the WLAN's tabs, and saving keeps the work after a reboot.

questions.question: In the WLC GUI, what is the purpose of a dynamic interface?
choices: It maps a WLAN to a wired VLAN and holds the DHCP server setting for its clients
It connects the WLC to the RADIUS server only
It is the interface used for CAPWAP tunnels to APs
questions.explanation: Dynamic interfaces connect WLANs to VLANs, each with its own IP address and DHCP server for relaying client requests. CAPWAP uses the management interface.

questions.question: Which three settings are part of configuring a WPA2-Personal WLAN on a WLC? (Choose three.)
choices: Layer 2 Security set to WPA+WPA2 with WPA2 Policy checked
Authentication Key Management set to PSK with a passphrase
A RADIUS server added on the AAA Servers tab
Web authentication on the Layer 3 tab
questions.explanation: WPA2-Personal needs WPA2 with AES and PSK key management. A RADIUS server is for 802.1X Enterprise mode, TKIP is deprecated, and Layer 3 web authentication is a different feature.

questions.question: An engineer creates a WLAN and sets a passphrase, but clients cannot join, and the WLANs page shows the security below. What was missed?
questions.code:
WLAN ID  Type  Profile Name  WLAN SSID  Admin Status  Security Policies
1        WLAN  Staff         Staff      Enabled       [WPA2][Auth(802.1X)]
choices: The WLAN must be disabled and re-enabled
Authentication Key Management is still 802.1X; it must be changed to PSK
The SSID must differ from the profile name
AES must be replaced with TKIP
questions.explanation: A new WLAN defaults to WPA2 with 802.1X. Auth(802.1X) means the WLAN expects RADIUS authentication; enabling PSK (and unchecking 802.1X) makes it show [WPA2][Auth(PSK)].

questions.question: A WLAN will carry mostly voice-over-Wi-Fi calls. Which QoS setting on the WLAN's QoS tab fits?
questions.explanation: Platinum is for voice, Gold for video, Silver (the default) for best effort and Bronze for background traffic.

questions.question: Clients associate to the new Staff WLAN using the correct passphrase, but they all receive 169.254.x.x addresses. The WLAN is mapped to the management interface instead of the Staff dynamic interface for VLAN 20. What is the best fix?
choices: Change the passphrase and reconnect the clients
Change the WLAN encryption from AES to TKIP
On the General tab, select the Staff dynamic interface for VLAN 20, and confirm its DHCP server
questions.explanation: Associating with the right passphrase proves the security works. The clients land in the wrong VLAN with no working DHCP path, so the WLAN must be mapped to the correct dynamic interface.

questions.question: A new WLAN is fully configured, but no client can see its SSID. Which cause is most likely?
choices: The WLAN's Status is not enabled, or Broadcast SSID is unchecked
The QoS level is set to Silver
questions.explanation: A disabled WLAN is not advertised, and with Broadcast SSID unchecked it does not appear in client lists. Passphrase and QoS settings do not affect whether the SSID is seen.

questions.question: An engineer on a laptop connected to the corporate WLAN cannot open the WLC's web GUI, although it works from a wired PC. What explains this?
choices: The WLC GUI only supports Internet Explorer
The WLC blocks management access from wireless clients by default
The laptop needs a static IP address
questions.explanation: By default a Cisco WLC does not allow management sessions that arrive through a WLAN, a deliberate security choice. It can be enabled globally with Management > Mgmt Via Wireless.

questions.question: A client sees the SSID but fails to authenticate to a WPA2-PSK WLAN. What would you check, and why are VLAN and DHCP not the first suspects?
questions.answer: Check the passphrase first, then that the client supports WPA2 with AES and that the WLAN uses PSK rather than 802.1X. VLAN and DHCP problems only appear after a client has authenticated, as associated clients with no valid IP address.
questions.explanation: Sorting symptoms into not visible, cannot authenticate and no IP address points you to the right part of the configuration.

questions.question: Which cipher does WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode require?
questions.explanation: The 192-bit mode uses GCMP-256 with 384-bit elliptic curve cryptography and SHA-384. Ordinary WPA3 modes use AES-CCMP-128, and TKIP and RC4 belong to WPA and WEP.

questions.question: A company wants to start using WPA3 but still has many WPA2-only laptops. What lets both kinds of client join the same SSID?
choices: WPA2/WPA3 transition mode, where WPA3 clients use SAE and WPA2 clients use the PSK
Using WEP for the older laptops
questions.explanation: Transition mode advertises both methods on one SSID with the same passphrase, and keeps PMF optional so WPA2 clients are not refused. TKIP and WEP would weaken the WLAN, and hiding the SSID changes nothing about security.

questions.question: Which two are required in WPA3-Personal? (Choose two.)
choices: SAE in place of the PSK exchange
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE and makes PMF mandatory. RADIUS and client certificates belong to Enterprise designs, and WPA3 does not allow TKIP.

questions.question: Which EAP method, developed by Cisco, uses a protected access credential (PAC) instead of requiring certificates?
questions.explanation: EAP-FAST builds its protected tunnel with a PAC. EAP-TLS needs certificates on both sides, and PEAP and EAP-TTLS use a server certificate.

questions.question: Put the steps of a client joining a WPA2-Enterprise WLAN on a Cisco WLC in order.
items: The client associates with the AP using open authentication
The WLC relays the EAP exchange between the client and the RADIUS server
The RADIUS server sends an Access-Accept with keying material for the PMK
The client and the authenticator run the 4-way handshake to derive the PTK and GTK
questions.explanation: Association comes first, then 802.1X/EAP proves the user's identity to the server, the accept delivers the PMK material, and the 4-way handshake turns it into session keys before any data is sent.

questions.question: Why should PEAP clients be configured to validate the RADIUS server's certificate?
choices: Otherwise an evil twin with its own RADIUS server can collect users' credentials
It is needed to pick the radio channel
questions.explanation: The server certificate is how the client knows it is talking to the real network. Without checking it, a fake AP with a fake RADIUS server receives the inner credentials.

questions.question: On an AireOS WLC, where do you define the RADIUS servers that a WPA2-Enterprise WLAN will use?
choices: Under Security > AAA > RADIUS > Authentication, then select them on the WLAN's Security > AAA Servers tab
Only on the WLAN's General tab
questions.explanation: Servers are defined globally with their IP address, shared secret and port, and each WLAN then chooses up to six of them on its AAA Servers tab.

questions.question: On a Catalyst 9800 controller, which object links a WLAN profile to a policy profile?
questions.explanation: A policy tag pairs WLAN profiles with policy profiles, and the tag is assigned to the APs that should broadcast those WLANs.

questions.question: On a Catalyst 9800, a new WLAN profile with WLAN ID 17 and a policy profile with VLAN 20 both exist, but no AP broadcasts the SSID. What is missing?
choices: A policy tag that pairs the two profiles, assigned to the APs
questions.explanation: The default policy tag only covers WLAN IDs 1 to 16, so WLAN 17 must be placed in a policy tag with its policy profile, and that tag must be on the APs. Dynamic interfaces are an AireOS concept.

questions.question: A user mistypes the WPA2 passphrase several times, then enters it correctly, but the laptop still cannot connect for about a minute. What explains this?
choices: The WLC's client exclusion policy blocked the client after repeated authentication failures, by default for 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Client exclusion temporarily blocks clients that fail authentication repeatedly, which slows password guessing. After the exclusion time the client can join with the right passphrase.

questions.question: With the default Advanced settings on an AireOS WLAN, how often must clients reauthenticate because of the session timeout?
questions.explanation: The default session timeout is 1800 seconds. When it expires the client must reauthenticate, which on a PSK WLAN happens quietly in the background.

questions.question: Match each wireless threat to the control that addresses it.

pairs.left: Eavesdropping on frames from the parking lot
pairs.right: AES encryption with WPA2 or WPA3

pairs.left: Offline guessing of a captured handshake
pairs.right: WPA3 SAE or a long random passphrase

pairs.left: An employee's unauthorized AP plugged into a wall jack
pairs.right: Rogue AP detection on the WLC

questions.explanation: Each threat has a specific answer: encryption for eavesdropping, PMF for forged management frames, SAE for offline guessing, and rogue detection for unauthorized APs.
